title: Think-Pair-Share for Mathematical Reasoning
preview: Students solve a problem individually, discuss their reasoning with a partner, then share strategies with the whole class.

body.summary: A structured discussion protocol where students first think independently about a math problem, then explain their reasoning to a partner, and finally share key ideas with the class. The goal is to make mathematical thinking visible — students practice articulating their reasoning before the pressure of whole-class sharing.
body.whenToUse:
Use during guided practice to check understanding of a new concept, or as a warm-up to activate prior knowledge. Especially effective after introducing a new problem-solving strategy, when you want to see how students are approaching a problem before moving on.

Avoid using when the problem has only one simple step — the discussion won't have enough substance. The problem should require at least 2-3 steps or have multiple valid approaches.
body.howToImplement:
1. THINK (1-2 min): Pose a problem on the board. Say: "Work on this silently on your own. I want to see your thinking on paper — not just the answer." Walk the room and observe approaches.

2. PAIR (2-3 min): Say: "Turn to your partner. Partner A, you have 90 seconds to explain your approach. Partner B, your job is to listen and ask one question. Then switch." Use a visible timer.

3. SHARE (3-5 min): Strategically select 2-3 pairs based on what you observed during the Think phase. Say: "I noticed some interesting strategies. [Name], can you share what you and your partner discussed?" Record strategies on the board.

4. CONNECT (1-2 min): Ask the class: "How are these strategies similar? Which one feels most efficient to you? Why?"
body.teacherMoves:
IF students are not writing during Think time:
→ Walk over and quietly say: "I need to see your thinking on paper. Even if you're stuck, write down what you know about the problem and what's confusing."
→ Provide a sticky note: "Write one thing you notice about this problem."

IF a pair is silent or off-topic:
→ Give them a starter: "Partner A, start by telling Partner B: 'The first thing I did was...'" 
→ Stand near them (proximity) and say: "I'm going to come back in 30 seconds to hear what you discussed."

IF one partner is dominating the conversation:
→ Interrupt and say: "Partner B, can you restate what Partner A just said in your own words?"
→ Use a physical signal (e.g., a talking chip) — you can only talk when you're holding the chip.

IF students say "I don't get it" during sharing:
→ Redirect: "That's okay — tell us what part you DO understand, and where you got stuck."
→ Ask the class: "Who can explain the first step in a different way?"

IF the whole class used the same strategy:
→ Say: "Everyone used the same approach — nice! Now let me show you a second way to think about this." Model an alternative and ask: "What are the advantages of each?"
body.variations:
TIER 1 (Core):
Use as described above. Rotate partners weekly so students hear different perspectives.

TIER 2 (Scaffolded):
Provide sentence frames on the desk or on the board:
• "I solved this by first ___, then I ___."
• "My answer is ___ because ___."
• "I agree/disagree with my partner because ___."
• "One thing I'm not sure about is ___."

Pre-select strategic partnerships (pair a mid-level student with a slightly-above student — avoid pairing highest with lowest). Give Tier 2 students a 1-minute head start on the Think phase.

TIER 2 (Alternative — Written Think-Pair-Share):
Instead of verbal sharing, students write their explanation on a whiteboard and swap boards with their partner. Partner reads, then writes one question or comment. This helps students who struggle with verbal processing.

ADVANCED EXTENSION:
Have pairs compare two different solution methods and evaluate: "Which strategy is more efficient? When might the other strategy be better?" Then write a brief justification.
body.researchBase: Lyman (1981) developed Think-Pair-Share as a cooperative learning strategy. Research shows it increases participation rates from ~15% to over 80% and improves mathematical reasoning when combined with accountable talk stems (Chapin, O'Connor, & Anderson, 2009). The National Council of Teachers of Mathematics recommends structured discourse as a core practice for developing mathematical proficiency.
